 Food recalls happen for predictable reasons, from contamination and mislabeling to packaging defects, and knowing them helps shoppers stay safer
 1 / 12 List slides From bacteria to bad seals: 10 reasons food recalls happen List slides Previous Start over By Colleen Cabili · Updated October 20, 2026 Add QZ to Google Illustration: Quartz
 Grocery shelves project a permanence that the supply chain behind them does not have. The Food and Drug Administration and the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service together oversee hundreds of food recalls each year. The scale ranges from a single regional lot of bagged lettuce to a nationwide withdrawal of a snack stocked in every major chain. Most of those notices never reach the evening news. Yet nearly all of them trace back to a short list of familiar failures.
 That pattern is the useful part. A recall notice is a dense, bureaucratic document, and the reason listed on it determines how a household should respond. Undeclared peanuts in a cookie demand immediate action from a family managing a nut allergy and pose no risk at all to anyone else. A net weight printed incorrectly on a label carries no health consequence whatsoever. A positive Listeria test on ready-to-eat deli meat applies to everyone in the house, and especially to pregnant people and older adults. Reading the stated cause tells a shopper whether to discard a product immediately, return it for a refund, or treat it as a minor labeling matter.
 The causes also cluster by food category in ways worth knowing. Leafy greens, soft cheeses, deli counters, and low-acid canned goods each carry recurring risks rooted in how they are grown, processed, or stored. Baby food has drawn intensified heavy metal testing. Packaged bakery items and snack mixes turn up often in allergen and labeling recalls, because they run on shared production lines and change recipes frequently.
 What follows breaks down the 10 reasons that appear most often in FDA and USDA recall records. They range from bacterial pathogens and mislabeled packages to seal failures, naturally occurring toxins, and gaps in supplier traceability. Each one marks a distinct point where a safety system breaks down — on a farm, inside a processing plant, on a packaging line, or in the handoffs between them. Taken together, they explain why no aisle in the store is exempt.
 Bacterial contamination 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Bacterial contamination is one of the most common reasons food gets pulled from store shelves, and three pathogens dominate the notices: Listeria monocytogenes, Salmonella, and E. coli O157:H7. All three cause illness that ranges from cramps and diarrhea to hospitalization, and E. coli O157:H7 can lead to kidney failure.
 Listeria accounts for an outsized share of recalls because it grows at refrigerator temperatures, which most foodborne bacteria cannot do. That resilience explains its recurring appearance in deli meats, soft cheeses, ice cream, smoked fish, and pre-cut produce such as cantaloupe. It is also the pathogen of greatest concern for pregnant people, newborns, adults over 65, and anyone with a weakened immune system.
 Salmonella turns up most often in poultry, eggs, raw flour, and low-moisture foods such as nut butters and spices. E. coli O157:H7 is tied closely to ground beef and leafy greens, romaine lettuce in particular. One contaminated animal or irrigation source can spread through a batch that gets ground, mixed, and shipped across many states.
 Entry points are consistent. Contaminated irrigation or processing water, weak sanitation inside a plant, and cross-contact between raw and ready-to-eat items on a shared line are the usual culprits. A facility handling raw chicken alongside bagged salads carries real risk when the cleaning routine between runs falls short.
 Detection comes from testing rather than observation, since contaminated food rarely looks or smells wrong. Manufacturers test finished product and swab equipment, floors, and drains as part of ongoing environmental monitoring. A single positive swab can pull an entire production lot covering weeks of output. The FDA and the Food Safety and Inspection Service run their own sampling programs and can press for a recall independent of the company.
 Illness from these organisms can take days or weeks to appear, and many cases never get reported to health authorities. A recall notice often arrives after the product has already been eaten. That delay is why health officials advise discarding or returning a recalled item rather than inspecting it first and deciding it looks fine.
 Undeclared allergens 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Undeclared allergens are the most common labeling-related reason food gets recalled in the U.S. The term means a package contains one of the nine major allergens — milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans, or sesame — without naming it on the label.
 Two separate failures produce these notices. In the first, the allergen belongs to the recipe but never reaches the ingredient statement. A supplier swaps in a whey-based thickener, or a reformulated sauce picks up soy, and the printed label stays frozen on the old formula.
 In the second, the recipe is clean and the production environment is not. Protein residue left on shared equipment carries into the batch that follows. A plain oat cookie can collect enough peanut protein from an earlier run to put an allergic customer in danger.
 Sesame became the ninth allergen requiring disclosure on January 1, 2023, under the FASTER Act. Manufacturers that had controlled the original eight for decades often had nothing equivalent in place for sesame, so cleaning validation, supplier documentation, and label review steps all had to be built from scratch.
 The health stakes set this category apart from recalls driven by quality or appearance. For a shopper without the allergy, the food is fine. For someone with it, anaphylaxis can begin within minutes and calls for epinephrine rather than watchful waiting. That asymmetry is why the FDA generally assigns undeclared allergen recalls its most serious classification, even when the product is otherwise safe to eat.
 Root causes tend to be procedural rather than biological. A label roll gets loaded onto the wrong line. A limited-edition flavor goes into existing packaging. A printing proof wins approval before the formula behind it is final. Each of those errors attaches to a specific shift, print run, or lot code. A manufacturer can usually pin down which cases shipped and when, which keeps the recall narrower than a pathogen investigation allows.
 Foreign object contamination 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Foreign object recalls cover anything physical that should never have been in the package: metal fragments, hard plastic shards, glass, bone chips, rubber gasket pieces, even wood splinters. The hazard is mechanical rather than microbial — cuts to the mouth and throat, broken teeth, and choking.
 Metal is the most frequently cited material, and it almost always comes off the machinery itself. Blades dull and chip, wire mesh screens fray, bolts loosen, and bearings wear down over thousands of hours of high-speed operation. Grinders handling frozen product work under particular stress, which is why ground meat and frozen vegetable lines appear regularly in this recall category.
 Plastic enters the same way. Conveyor belting abrades, scrapers crack, and the protective guards around mixers and hoppers turn brittle and snap. A fragment that drops into a vat of dough or sauce disperses through the batch without a trace, and nothing about the finished product looks wrong on the line.
 Glass is less common but draws sharper regulatory attention because of the injury potential. Sources include jars that shatter during filling, unshielded overhead light fixtures, and sight gauges on processing tanks. Plants that handle glass containers generally maintain written breakage procedures and a log of every incident for that reason.
 Many of these recalls begin with a consumer rather than a lab. Someone bites down on something hard, calls the number printed on the package or files a report with the FDA, and the manufacturer cannot rule out that other units from the same lot carry the same defect. That uncertainty is what forces the recall.
 Prevention runs on detection equipment. In-line metal detectors reject contaminated units automatically, and X $TWTR -ray systems extend that coverage to dense plastic, glass, bone, and stone, which metal detectors miss entirely. Both need scheduled calibration checks using test pieces of a known size.
 Recalls in this category tend to be narrower than pathogen recalls. Once a plant identifies the broken part, it can usually pinpoint when the failure started and limit the recall to production after that point rather than weeks of output.
 Mislabeling and incorrect packaging 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A mislabeling recall means the package does not match its contents. The label may be accurate in itself but applied to the wrong product, or it may carry incorrect nutrition data, an understated net weight, or a country-of-origin statement that does not reflect where the food was grown or produced.
 Packaging mix-ups on high-speed lines account for a large share of these cases. A plant that fills barbecue sauce and then switches to spicy mustard has to change labels at exactly the right moment. If the changeover runs a few seconds early or late, jars leave the line under the wrong name. A shopper opens what the label describes as mild and finds a different ingredient list, a different heat level and, in some cases, a different allergen profile.
 Labeling rules make even low-risk versions of this problem actionable. FDA and USDA regulations require packaging to state ingredients, allergens and nutrition information accurately, so a misprinted serving size or an incorrect weight declaration can prompt a recall whether or not anyone could get sick from the product.
 Private label manufacturing spreads a single error across many retailers at once. One facility often produces the same item sold under dozens of store brand names, so one bad print run or misapplied label there can surface as separate recall notices from chains that appear to have no connection to each other. A shopper might see several unrelated-looking announcements in the same week, all originating from one plant and one shift.
 The FDA sorts recalls by the health risk they pose rather than by the type of error that caused them. A missing allergen declaration lands in the most serious class, because the omission can trigger a severe reaction in someone who reads the label and relies on it. An inaccurate weight statement or a typographical flaw in the nutrition panel usually falls into a lower class, since the result is a consumer getting something other than what was advertised rather than something medically hazardous. The classification printed on a recall notice is the fastest way to tell which of the two situations applies.
 Chemical contamination 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Chemical contamination recalls involve substances that do not belong in food at the levels found. Three categories dominate: pesticide residue above legal tolerances, cleaning and sanitizing agents left on equipment, and heavy metals such as lead, arsenic, and cadmium. Laboratory analysis, not visual inspection, catches nearly all of them.
 Pesticide cases usually involve a crop treated with a compound not approved for it, or residue above the tolerance the Environmental Protection Agency sets for that pesticide and commodity pairing. The FDA tests imported and domestic foods for residues, and the USDA runs its own sampling program. A sample that exceeds its tolerance can prompt a recall with no illness reports attached, because the legal threshold itself is the trigger.
 Sanitizer residue tends to come from a sequencing error rather than a design flaw. A caustic cleaning solution is not fully rinsed from a tank before the next batch runs through. Sometimes a chemical drum sits too close to an open line and leaks. Consumer complaints can surface these incidents before the plant does. Quaternary ammonium compounds and chlorine-based sanitizers leave a sharp chemical taste or a burning sensation that is hard to miss.
 Heavy metals follow a different path. Lead, arsenic, and cadmium occur naturally in soil, and crops including rice, carrots, and sweet potatoes draw them up through their roots during normal growth. No one adds them, and no cleaning protocol removes them. Baby food and toddler snacks have drawn the most regulatory scrutiny. The developing nervous system is more vulnerable to these exposures, and infants eat a narrow range of foods in large amounts relative to their body weight. The FDA's Closer to Zero initiative set action levels for lead in several baby food categories, giving regulators a defined number against which a batch can fail.
 The detection gap shapes how these recalls unfold. A plant can run its standard quality checks and find nothing, because residues and metals require targeted laboratory assays that sit outside routine production testing. Government surveillance sampling often identifies the problem first, which means the manufacturer hears about it from a regulator rather than from its own lab.
 Underprocessing and improper canning 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Underprocessing means a canned or jarred food was not heated hot enough, or long enough, to destroy spores of Clostridium botulinum, the bacterium that produces botulinum toxin. Low-acid canned goods — vegetables, fish, soups, and commercially packed preserves — are where this failure turns up most often.
 The risk comes from the environment inside a sealed container. Clostridium botulinum spores survive boiling water temperatures and germinate in low-oxygen, low-acid conditions, which is exactly what a sealed can provides. Destroying them takes pressure-based thermal processing well above 212 degrees Fahrenheit, held for a validated length of time. Acidic products such as pickles, tomatoes with added acid, and most fruit juices do not need that treatment, because the acidity alone keeps the spores from growing.
 Commercial canners work from a filed process schedule that sets the temperature, duration, container size, and fill weight required for a given product. Several failures can leave live spores in finished goods. A retort that never reaches its set point, a timer error, an overfilled can, or a batch pushed through during a documented process deviation will each do it.
 Nothing about the result is visible. A can that was underprocessed looks, smells, and tastes entirely normal.
 That absence of warning signs is why regulators treat these recalls as urgent. Spoilage organisms usually announce themselves through off odors or visible mold. Botulinum toxin does not, and ingesting it can cause blurred vision, slurred speech, and descending paralysis that reaches the muscles controlling breathing.
 Under the FDA's low-acid canned food regulations, processors must register their facilities, file scheduled processes with the agency, and keep time-and-temperature records for every batch. Records are the enforcement lever. When a company cannot document that a lot met its filed schedule, a recall can follow without any laboratory confirmation of contamination, because the missing proof is itself the problem. Inspectors reviewing retort charts after the fact have prompted recalls of product that was never tested and may never have been contaminated.
 Equipment malfunctions and cross-contamination 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Machinery that fails mid-production triggers recalls because the failure moves contamination into food that was otherwise made correctly. A sanitation step cut short between runs, a refrigeration unit that quits on a delivery route, or an inspection system drifting out of calibration can each compromise a product without changing how it looks.
 Shared production lines carry the clearest version of this risk. A plant that runs a peanut-containing item and a peanut-free item on the same equipment depends entirely on the cleaning cycle between them. When that cycle is shortened to hit a production quota, or run with the wrong procedure, residue carries forward into the next batch. The recipe is correct. The equipment introduced the problem.
 Temperature control failures work on a different timeline. Perishable food held between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit sits in the range where bacteria multiply fastest, a window food safety agencies call the danger zone. A cooler that loses compressor function overnight in a warehouse, or a trailer refrigeration unit that fails partway through a multi-stop route, can expose a full pallet. Appearance rarely changes. Companies often catch the lapse only when a temperature log is reviewed or a data logger packed inside the shipment is downloaded after delivery.
 Inspection equipment degrades too. Metal detectors and X $TWTR -ray units require scheduled verification against test pieces of known size, and a unit that falls out of tolerance may keep running without sounding an alarm. Several shifts of output can clear the line before a routine check catches the drift, which is why recall notices citing this cause sometimes cover unusually wide production windows.
 Recalls rooted in equipment tend to produce consequences beyond the affected lot. Regulators read a mechanical or procedural breakdown as evidence about a facility's whole quality system rather than one batch. Corrective action plans commonly include retraining line staff, shortening calibration intervals, replacing worn components, and revalidating sanitation procedures.
 The paperwork changes as well. A plant that pulls product for a cleaning failure typically has to document a written changeover protocol, assign responsibility for verifying it, and keep records showing the step was completed on every run.
 Packaging defects and seal failures 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A container that fails to seal properly can turn safe food unsafe, which is why broken seams, pinhole leaks, and faulty closures account for a steady share of recall notices. Food processed correctly can still be contaminated after the fact, through the package rather than the recipe.
 Hermetically sealed products depend on an unbroken barrier. When a can's seam or the heat seal on a retort pouch does not form completely, oxygen and bacteria reach contents engineered to exclude both. Clostridium botulinum can then grow in low-acid, low-oxygen food. The toxin risk matches what a canning error produces, but it arrives through a mechanical defect rather than a processing one. Recall notices for canned goods sometimes name seam integrity or an incomplete seal as the stated cause.
 Flexible packaging fails differently. Dried fruit, snack mixes, shredded cheese, and pet food travel in laminated bags that can develop a pinhole from a sharp product edge, a jammed conveyor, or rough handling in transit. Air and moisture enter through an opening too small to see. Mold or rancidity then develops well ahead of the printed date.
 Visible damage gives shoppers something concrete to check. Recall notices for canned products often describe the warning signs: swelling, leaking, rust, or deep denting. Damage along a can's seam or rim warrants more concern than a dent in the flat middle of the body, since the seam does the sealing. A bulging lid on a jar signals gas production inside, and the contents should not be opened or tasted.
 Glass packaging adds a second failure mode. A jar or bottle that cracks during filling, capping, or shipping can break the seal and introduce fragments into the food at the same time, which is why some recalls cite breakage rather than a seal defect.
 Manufacturers check for these problems with seal strength tests, vacuum verification, and measurement of seam dimensions. A seamer that drifts out of adjustment, or a worn sealing bar on a pouch line, can turn out thousands of defective units before a quality check registers the change. Because the defect is mechanical and continuous, a recall often covers everything made between two inspections rather than one lot.
 Natural toxins from mold and improper fish handling 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Some recalls trace back to toxins that food generates on its own, with nothing introduced at a plant. Two dominate the records: aflatoxin, produced by mold on grains and nuts, and scombrotoxin, the histamine that accumulates in fish left too warm after the catch.
 Aflatoxin comes from Aspergillus molds that colonize corn, peanuts, pistachios, and other tree nuts held in warm, humid storage. The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies naturally occurring aflatoxins as carcinogenic to humans, and the FDA sets action levels capping how much may appear in food and in animal feed. Testing is routine in grain and nut handling, and a lot measured above the limit gets pulled. Drought stress during the growing season leaves crops more open to the mold before harvest, so the problem can begin in a field rather than a warehouse.
 Scombrotoxin, also called histamine fish poisoning, affects species carrying high natural levels of the amino acid histidine — tuna, mahi-mahi, mackerel, amberjack, and bluefish among them. Bacteria on the flesh convert that histidine into histamine when the fish is not chilled fast enough after it is landed. Cooking, canning, and freezing do not break histamine back down. Someone who eats affected fish can develop flushing, headache, rash, and gastrointestinal upset, often within an hour, a reaction that resembles an allergic response without involving allergy at all.
 Neither toxin announces itself. Fish loaded with histamine usually looks and smells acceptable, and nuts above the aflatoxin action level give no visual clue. Prevention sits far upstream: rapid icing on the boat and an unbroken cold chain for seafood, moisture and temperature control in storage for grains and nuts. Laboratory analysis is the only dependable check. Recalls in this category are frequently issued on test results alone, before a single illness is reported, and they can cover large volumes, because one contaminated lot of nuts or one mishandled shipment of tuna may already sit inside many different finished products.
 Supplier and ingredient traceability failures 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A traceability failure means a company cannot quickly identify which of its batches contain a suspect ingredient. It also covers the case where one shared supplier contaminates several brands at once, and nobody connects them until an outbreak investigation does. The resulting recalls tend to be broad, slow, and scattered across companies with no obvious link to each other.
 A single packaged meal can draw ingredients from dozens of suppliers across several countries. One contaminated raw input — diced onions, cucumbers, a spice powder, a nut butter base — can flow into salsas, dressings, seasoning blends, and refrigerated entrees made by unrelated manufacturers. None of those companies necessarily know they share a vendor. The common thread surfaces only when investigators work backward from a cluster of illnesses.
 That backward trace is the slow part. Health officials interview patients, identify a suspected food, then follow it through retailers, distributors, and processors to the originating farm or plant. Each handoff depends on the records the previous company kept. Strong documentation can narrow the search to a single shipment date within days. Weak documentation stretches the same work into weeks, and the ingredient keeps moving the whole time.
 Recordkeeping quality also determines how much product gets pulled. A manufacturer using lot numbers, batch codes, and digital inventory tracking can isolate the production runs that received the suspect ingredient and recall only those. A manufacturer without that detail often has to recall everything made over a wide window, because it cannot prove which batches were clean.
 The Food Safety Modernization Act, signed into law in 2011, pushed the industry toward tighter recordkeeping. It also gave the FDA authority to require tracing records for designated high-risk foods. Those rules have sped up some investigations without resolving the structural problem underneath them. A single ingredient can still pass through a grower, a processor, a broker, and a co-packer before it reaches a finished product. A gap at any one of those steps slows everything downstream.
